newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan arrests two Chinese for illicit bank network.
newsitem.headline: Japan arrests two Chinese for illicit bank network.

text.p: Japanese police have arrested two illegal Chinese immigrants for running an "underground bank" which thousands of fellow aliens used to sent $108 million back to China, police said on Tuesday.

The covert financial network in Yokohama, a port city near Tokyo with a thriving old Chinatown, highlights Japan's problem with illegal immigrants from China as it grapples with record numbers of arrivals this year.

Wu Tinjiang, 30, and He Jie, 33, -- Chinese nationals already on trial for illegal entry -- were arrested on Monday on suspicion of helping about 3,000 other Chinese illegally send some 12.6 billion yen ($108 million) to China between December 1995 and last February, a police spokesman said.

The two charged 0.5 percent commission for transferring funds to China on behalf of fellow illegal aliens, unable to transfer funds home legally because bank transactions require valid immigration papers.

He and Wu relayed orders from Japan to collaborators in China's southeastern Fujian province, who delivered cash from a fund to designated recipients. After the cash was delivered, the two men would wire payments to a Hong Kong bank account under the name of someone with a legal account in Japan.

Police suspect that in addition to transferring earnings by illegal labourers drawn to Japan for wages many times what they could earn in China, the underground banking network laundered cash from gambling and robbery rings.

Japan this year has caught unprecedented numbers of Chinese attempting to sneak into the country, with those caught in January and February alone topping all of those apprehended in 1996, an immigration official said.
As of the end of last month, 861 Chinese illegals had been caught, more than 80 percent of all would-be illegal immigrants, the official said.
Police admit the number may only represent one-tenth of those who successfully sneak into Japan.
In addition, 38,000 Chinese entered Japan legally but overstayed their visas as of the first day of this year, according to Justice Ministry figures.

The discovery of the banking network reinforces suspicions that labour smugglers have established a sophisticated network in Japan, using fake travel documents and a fleet of small boats with ultra-modern navigation equipment to evade maritime patrols, police said.

They lure people from Fujian Province and other densely-populated coastal Chinese provinces with the promise of high-paying factory jobs, typically charging three million yen ($25,800) for the passage, would-be immigrants have said.
The tide of Chinese illegal immigrants has sparked worries of increasing inter-Chinese crimes after several killings and other violent attacks involving the group in the past year.
In February Japan's Foreign Ministry asked China to crack down on the traffic.

Japan, with thousands of islands and a long coast, has been targeted by the immigrant smugglers because of a slower economy in Taiwan and uncertainty about Hong Kong with the approach of the British colony's return to Chinese sovereignty next month.
